idiom_name: boundary object with a domestic interface + injected connection wrapper
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the interface the application wants (verbs in the domestic vocabulary, parameters and results in domestic types), then implement it by translating into the foreign call and translating the answer back. Keep a separate connection wrapper that performs the actual foreign invocation (URL building, protocol, credentials, serialisation) and inject it, so the same gateway can be exercised against a test double. Confine the class to translation: mapping foreign fields, units, identifiers and error codes is its job; policy (retry vs fail, fallback, business rules) belongs to the connection, a decorator around the gateway, or the caller. Expose coarse-grained operations where a caller would otherwise loop, and never let foreign types appear in the gateway's own signature.
pitfalls: Skipping the connection separation and calling the foreign API directly from the gateway methods removes the test seam and mixes transport with translation.
Letting the gateway accumulate business rules turns it into a god object every feature has to change.
Exposing foreign identifiers, DTOs or raw payloads in the gateway's interface: the rest of the system then depends on the foreign context anyway.
Embedding a loop that calls the remote service per item without batching, causing an N+1 latency trap hidden behind a clean domestic method name.
Adding caching and retry logic directly inside the gateway class instead of in a decorator or injected connection, so the gateway violates single responsibility.
Returning the raw vendor DTO from a gateway method because 'the caller needs the data anyway', coupling the caller to the foreign schema and defeating the translation boundary.
Creating a separate gateway subclass per caller instead of sharing one gateway with an injected connection, causing per-client translation drift.

Wrong move: use a gateway as the system's business-workflow orchestrator -> domain rules and failure semantics become coupled to transport deployments -> instead keep orchestration in an application service and let the gateway translate calls and errors.

Wrong move: route every client through one universal gateway -> unrelated bounded contexts share a bottleneck and release owner -> instead use one gateway per cohesive external context or a focused backend-for-frontend when client needs differ.

Wrong move: add an API gateway before a real boundary problem exists -> an extra hop, configuration surface and failure domain add cost without reducing coupling -> instead start with a direct client or thin wrapper and introduce a gateway when repeated translation or cross-cutting policy justifies it.
